articles.headline: Ryan Day's buyout details: Here's how much it will cost Ohio State to fire head coach
keyFacts: Ohio State is experiencing its worst season in decades with four losses, drawing attention to head coach Ryan Day's contract.
Day signed a seven-year contract extension in February 2025 that pays him an annual salary of $12.5 million.
CBS Sports reported that firing Day after the 2026 season would cost Ohio State a buyout of $57.5 million.
body: The Ohio State Buckeyes are having their worst season in decades, as they enter Rivalry Week vs. Michigan with four losses. 2026 marks the first time since 2011 that OSU has more than three losses, and is the second time since 2004 if the Buckeyes get a win over Michigan.
Given OSU's down season, there is renewed attention surrounding head coach Ryan Day's contract. Day, who is in his eighth season as OSU's head coach, has never had a season worse than this one.
Let's take a look at where Day's contract stands with Ohio State, and what it would cost the school to fire him.
Ryan Day contract details
After Ohio State won a national championship last season under Day, the school rewarded him with a new seven-year contract extension that runs through 2031 in February 2025.

The deal bumped his annual salary to $12.5 million a year, which includes several bonus incentives. According to On3Sports, Day is making $12.6 million during the 2026 season, which makes him the fourth-highest paid coach in the country.
Day checks in behind Georgia's Kirby Smart ($13.3 million), Indiana's Curt Cignetti ($13 million) and LSU's Lane Kiffin ($13 million).
Ryan Day buyout details

According to CBS Sports, Day's contract states that instead of being owed a certain percentage of his contract, he would be paid $11.5 million per year left on his deal. That puts Day's buyout at $57.5 million if Ohio State chose to move on from Day after the 2026 season.
Ryan Day coaching record

Ryan Day has an 89-16 overall record at Ohio State, which is fourth in all-time wins in Ohio State history, behind Woody Hayes, John Cooper and Jim Tressel. He is just 17 games behind Tressel in his ninth season.

He also has led the Buckeyes to five College Football Playoff victories, including the four Ohio State had on its run to winning the 2024-25 CFP national championship. That season, the Buckeyes won four games against Top-10 teams.

articles.headline: Louisville's buzzer-beater ends St. John's comeback try: Five takeaways from craziest Players Era game to date
keyFacts: Louisville defeated St. John's 93-90 on Thursday after guard Adrian Wooley hit a game-winning 3-pointer at the buzzer.
The game marked St. John's coach Rick Pitino's first matchup against Louisville since he was fired from the school in 2017.
Louisville will play Tennessee on Friday for an opportunity to compete in the Players Era 16 championship game on Saturday.
body: LAS VEGAS — The craziest game of the first month of the college basketball season transpired when most of you who are reading this had likely fallen asleep from eating way too much on Thanksgiving.
To those who missed this ending in real time: I hope you learned your lesson. Never check out early on tournament hoops during turkey week. The best stuff often happens at the latest hours.

Fortunately, yours truly was courtside at Michelob Ultra Arena on Thursday night to see No. 25 Louisville's theatric, buzzer-beating 93-90 win against No. 13 St. John's, handing Rick Pitino's team his first loss of the season. The win was all the more dramatic because it was Pitino's former school beating his current one in a game that was loaded with controversy, confusion, a huge comeback/collapse, some incredible performances and instantly viral moments.

Adrian Wooley's 3-pointer from the left corner on a broken play got U of L its second straight win against a ranked opponent. Here's how the junior shooting guard kept the Cards alive for the Players Era 16 title at 8:29 p.m. local time on the Strip.
Jackpot.
"We played great defense, he made a lucky shot," Pitino said.
Cardinals coach Pat Kelsey called it a shot Woolely will "tell his grandkids about."
Wooley said it felt like a movie.
Typically, a good game happens and there's a column to write with a focused angle.

That's not happening here. Way too much attached, so I'm going to try and touch on all the relevant angles tied to this one before Louisville plays No. 9 Tennessee on Friday (9 p.m. ET on ESPN) for the opportunity to win Saturday's Players Era 16 championship.
1. Wooley's trey saved Cards from an epic choke

For most of the game, it looked like Louisville was going to give St. John's a loss at UConn. Louisville scored 57 of its 93 points in the first half, the 57-39 difference marking the largest halftime deficit St. John's has been a part of since Pitino became coach. It was also the most points in a half Pitino's team has allowed since he's been with SJU.
Cards showed up ready to play; St. John's looked like it was recovering from a Vegas hangover.

Then the full-court press started to work and a 20-3 St. John's run in the final four minutes got the game to toss-up status. The stifling defense combined with some Johnnies-on-the-spot buckets led to unexpected drama at a point when the game should've been decided. Ruben Prey's 3-pointer from the left wing with 20 seconds left cut it to a 90-88 Louisville lead.

Louisville avoided overtime with the winning shot on the final possession after two St. John's free throws from Ian Jackson tied the game at 90. (Don't worry, I'm getting to that near-catastrophe in the next section.)
Here's another look at Wooley's wily winner.
The triple was just Wooley's 10th made 3-pointer of the season.
"Once I made the shot and I turned around, there was a kid standing right there and I felt like I was just staring into his soul," Wooley said when asked about the play. "It was like a movie."
2. Officials dodge scandal, request for explanation

Had St. John's found a way to come back from 24 points down to win this game, the Louisville collapse would've been overlooked because we would've had an officiating scandal that might have taken over the weekend in college sports.

Official Tommy Johnson — according to what I saw and heard with my own eyes and ears, in addition to what ESPN's cameras caught and dozens of fans in the immediate vicinity of the play saw — incorrectly ruled that Louisville guard Jackson Shelstad called for a timeout with 13.7 seconds remaining and Louisville holding a 90-88 lead.

And wouldn't you know it, someone sitting courtside also caught the sequence on video. Watch and listen closely and you'll see that Shelstad doesn't call for timeout; this was just a gaffe by the official.

The problem with calling a timeout is that Louisville didn't have any left, so that results in a technical foul and two free throws for the other team. Despite pleas from Louisville's bench (and plenty of fans in the arena), the officials didn't correct the mistake. Jackson made both foul shots, tying the game at 90.

Then there was another twist: Louisville received the ball, by rule. That came as a surprise to Louisville's coaching staff. Kelsey said in the postgame press conference he thought St. John's would get the ball. Even Pitino indicated he thought SJU would get the ball.
Instead, Louisville got the ball with 13.7 to go on what wound up being the final possession of the game. Wooley's 3-pointer was as much of a ball-don't-lie vindication as you'll ever see.
The Athletic's CJ Moore approached the game officials afterward and requested a comment; the crew declined.
That's not acceptable, not when a blown call is obvious and could have flipped a game result.
The call was so egregious, it prompted Kelsey to mime an attentive dog's pose.

Refs owning up to mistakes and/or offering insight as to why calls do or don't get made in crucial end-game moments isn't an easy thing to do, but it should be the proper protocol. Had this been a conference or NCAA postseason game, we would've gotten more because of established procedures. Nonconference games allow officials to defiantly dodge media inquiries.
3. Pitino claims the matchup wasn't personal
The big story going into this game, of course, was Pitino facing Louisville for the first time since he was fired in October 2017.
Pitino was asked about it in the postgame press conference, but given everything else that was involved in the game, this plot point wasn't nearly as prominent in the aftermath.

"I didn't have any, to be perfectly honest with you," Pitino said when asked about any strong emotions going into Thursday night. Now, if I was coaching in the Yum! Center, I think I'd have a lot. But it's just a terrific Louisville basketball team that we're trying to beat — no different than trying to beat Kentucky last year. ... I love the fans of Louisville, proud of what Pat Kelsey's doing with the team."

I can't buy that Pitino wasn't in his feels over this game on some level. Playing Louisville in Las Vegas on Thanksgiving and with a crowd of maybe 3,500 on hand definitely made it easier because it wasn't in a hostile home/road environment.

But it's still Louisville. And Louisville represents the longest coaching tenure of his Hall of Fame career. He wanted to win this game, I'm sure, as much as any regular season opportunity he's had since getting back into college coaching in 2021. He had one hint at that desire.

"Things didn't go right for us in the first half but when we were down 12, I said we are going to win this game," Pitino said. "I couldn't be more proud of our basketball team in the way they fought back with incredible hustle, incredible desire to win."

Kelsey, on the other hand, said it was an honor to face Pitino. You could hear the reverence in his voice. He said Pitino is maybe the greatest college coach of all time and referred to Pitino's patented full-court press as the best ever in the sport. Kelsey even apologized to Pitino's face for celebrating too hard at Wooley's game-winner, then having to stiffen up for the handshake line.
"It was an honor to coach against him," Kelsey said.
4. Game was a microcosm of courtroom implications

Oh, by the way: Seth Trimble had his best game as a college player on Thursday. He finished with a career-high 33 points off the bench and was the reason Louisville won, even with Wooley's incredible shot. That play, per Kelsey, was supposed to be for Trimble to get into the paint and have a shot close to the rim.
So it was 33 points instead of 35.
"We got dominated by a great point guard tonight," Pitino said.

Trimble, who is in his fifth season, is only playing because a judge has allowed him to do so against the wishes of the NCAA. Kelsey made huge headlines for his public display on the stand in defense of Trimble back in October. If that doesn't happen, Louisville likely isn't 2-0 at Players Era through Thursday and 6-1 overall. Trimble wasn't the only guy playing on Thursday night in this game who needed a friendly judge to see the floor, either.
St. John's has multiple.
Keyshawn Hall is one of them. He had 17 points and 10 rebounds for St. John's. Babacar Sane is another. He finished with 14 points for SJU.

Given all that, I couldn't help but think that this game will prove be a microcosm of what we're going to see all season long. Teams will win big games, earn conference titles, good NCAA seeds and make the Final Four because of rulings made in their favor by judges.
Pitino took time to criticize the NCAA's end-of-June timing for changing the five-for-five rule. It's led to inconsistency across college sports.

"All that had to happen with all of this is come out with a ruling in November and December," Pitino said. "Why do it in the summer when all this money is involved? You knew that was going to happen, so it was mind-boggling that you could make such a traumatic mistake like that."
5. St. John's, Baylor screwed on scheduling
Scheduling two eight-team tournaments in two arenas with similar tip times means that adjusting for the winners' and losers' brackets will lead to a tight turnaround or two.

But St. John's has to play Iowa State at 10 a.m. local time in the third-place game of the MUA (Michelob Ultra Arena) bracket on Friday. There will be people that read this story about the Louisville-SJU game after St. John's tips against the Cyclones. The turnaround is all of 13.5 hours, which is egregious.

ESPN and Players Era organizers had to agree on the bracket format, of course, and TV's role in trying to maximize viewership with coinciding tournaments inevitably meant that a couple of teams were going to get squeezed on the third day of games. But asking any team to play on less than at least 16 hours worth of rest isn't justifiable. Pitino took issue with it, noting that Iowa State will prep with almost nine hours more rest, but also refused to allow for any excuses.

"I don't think the tournament was very intelligent to have us turn around and play at 10 o'clock in the morning," Pitino said, then added, "if Iowa State beats us, it's not because we weren't ready to play. We will be ready."

The same is true of Baylor, which lost just before 11 p.m. West Coast time on Thursday night against Gonzaga and will only get 13 hours before it faces TCU at noon local time Friday at T-Mobile Arena.

Both games are third-place games in their respective brackets. Why they have to be so early is strange. This isn't nearly as problematic as last year's 18-team Players Era field that couldn't be in a bracketed format, but it is one more tweak that needs to be addressed in 2027.

articles.headline: Familiar faces and surprise chances as Ireland face Wallabies
keyFacts: Ireland head coach Andy Farrell made two enforced line-up changes for Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off against Australia.
Jacob Stockdale replaces ill Mack Hansen and Nick Timoney replaces banned Dan Sheehan in Ireland's starting team.
Captain Tadhg Beirne said Ireland must keep delivering in big games to build belief before next year's World Cup.
body: Tadhg Beirne is hoping to lead Ireland to a fourth win from as many games this month [Getty Images] Discussion about how Ireland head coach Andy Farrell would approach Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off against Australia was ended emphatically by the team announcement on Wednesday.

While Farrell would have been excused for fielding a rotated side in the wake of last week's bruising victory over world champions South Africa , he instead opted for continuity and is challenging his first-choice line-up to produce another chest-thumping 80-minute display against the Wallabies.
Farrell has made two changes from the side that started Saturday's 20-17 success over the Springboks in Dublin, both of which are enforced.
Jacob Stockdale replaces the ill Mack Hansen on the left wing while in-form back row Nick Timoney is restored at number eight in place of the banned Dan Sheehan.
While Ireland cannot win the inaugural Nations Championship, Farrell has emphasised the importance of Friday in the context of the team's journey to next year's World Cup.
A win over Australia would be four wins in as many weekends. Do that down under next year and Ireland will find themselves in another World Cup quarter-final.

The six-day turnaround between last week's win over South Africa and Friday's contest with Australia serves as useful preparation for next year's tournament, where Ireland will have six days between their pool games against Portugal and Scotland and potentially a quarter and semi-final, should they reach that stage.
With no six-day turnarounds in the 2027 Six Nations, Farrell is keen to test his side within those parameters before they return to their provinces for a busy festive schedule.
Farrell picks side to 'back up' South Africa win
Stockdale returns as Ireland make two changes
Sheehan out of Wallabies Test after two-game ban
While the World Cup unavoidably edges into view, Ireland's immediate priority is to close out a largely positive 2026 on a winning note.

Sobering defeats by France and New Zealand cast doubts over the squad's trajectory, but last week's narrow win over South Africa served as a reminder that Farrell's side can still mix it with the world's best.
And while slaying the Springboks may have restored hope among fans, senior squad figures have carefully tempered expectations as they attempt to round out the year with a 10th win from 12 Tests.

"If you're winning games by the skin of your teeth and not performing well you don't really gain that belief, but when you're playing well and then start winning well the belief comes and that's something that we certainly gained before the 2023 World Cup," said Tadhg Beirne, who will captain Ireland against Australia in Sheehan's absence.

"But we're building that and we're often talking about that in terms of creating that belief, creating that identity that we want to see of ourselves, but again we're nowhere near where we need to be if we want to be competing to win a World Cup next year.
"I think there's so much more growth but we have to keep delivering in these big games for everyone to feel it and I know how it feels back in 2023 going into that World Cup.

"I think everyone in that squad felt it and I think we're certainly on the way there and if we can keep performing the way we've been performing but getting better we'll certainly be there by next year."
Can Stockdale seize his chance?
Friday night is a big opportunity for Stockdale, who was not involved in the wins over Argentina, Fiji and South Africa.
Nearly nine years removed from his star-making performances for Joe Schmidt's Ireland in the 2018 Grand Slam campaign, the 30-year-old Ulster wing is no longer a nailed-on starter.

But having been picked ahead of Tommy O'Brien - who scored two tries in the win over Fiji - Stockdale must seize an opportunity to impress on what will be his first run-out at Twickenham since a try-scoring cameo off the bench in a behind-closed-doors Autumn Nations Cup defeat by England in November 2020.

Stockdale needn't look far for inspiration. Seven of his Ulster team-mates are in the matchday 23. Two of them - Stuart McCloskey and Timoney - have featured in all 12 Tests this year (alongside Beirne), while jet-heeled right winger Robert Baloucoune is enjoying his best run as an international after a couple of tries against South Africa last week.
In January 2016, Stockdale made his Ulster debut under the province's then director of rugby Les Kiss, the man now leading the Wallabies.

The 61-year-old replaced Schmidt following the July leg of the Nations Championship, and while scrutiny on the Queenslander intensified following defeats by England and Scotland, last week's 29-26 victory over Wales has boosted the Wallaby morale as they attempt to snap a six-game losing streak against the Irish.

Kiss, who was Ireland's defence coach during the historic 2009 Grand Slam triumph, has turned heads with his own selection in the number 11 jersey, with former Northampton Saints winger James Ramm earning his Test debut at the age of 28.
Kurtley Beale - who started Australia's last victory over Ireland in June 2018 - is an eye-catching addition to the bench as the 37-year-old closes in on a first Test cap in five years.
With Kalani Thomas earning a first start at scrum-half and a new back-row combination in Tom Hooper, Carlo Tizzano and Rob Valetini, it is an intriguing Wallabies line-up.

But if Ireland can replicate the intensity and edge they showed against South Africa, they may pass Farrell's World Cup rehearsal and ensure they approach the tantalising possibilities of 2027 in buoyant form.

articles.headline: Volvo's big batteries: We drive its updated 2028 plug-in hybrids
keyFacts: Volvo updated its XC60 and XC90 plug-in hybrid vehicles for model year 2028 with larger batteries and modern infotainment systems.
The automaker refreshed the existing models instead of developing all-new replacements because global electrification rates vary across key markets.
The updated plug-in hybrids are currently in production and will reach the first US customers in the first quarter of next year.
body: COPENHAGEN, Denmark—If we lived in the world that Volvo’s product planners expected back when the current XC90 debuted in 2015, both it and the smaller but related XC60 (which arrived in 2017) might have been the last of their kind as everything went electric. As we know, the future hasn’t turned out quite like that, especially in the critically important US market. At the same time, Europe and China are electrifying, which seems like an argument against spending resources on developing all-new replacements for models that might not have an eight-year lifespan in most markets.

So instead, Volvo has given the XC60 and XC90 another lifecycle refresh. The exterior styling tweaks are minimal; the bigger three-row XC90 had already been given a new look last year, and the XC60 now gains a similar grille and the same matrix headlights, for instance. And that’s no bad thing—both were, and remain, handsome shapes that are popular with Volvo’s customer base.

Instead, the Swedish automaker’s attention has been on bringing the technology up to date for model year 2028 standards. Which means a much bigger battery for the PHEVs, with sufficient capacity for a couple of days of daily driving for most of us before needing to be recharged. There’s also new, modern infotainment and interiors that are now even nicer to spend time in than before.

We first saw the revamped 2028 XC60 (and learned about its technical details and those of the XC90) in September, but with the cars going into production now and due to reach the first US customers in the first quarter of next year, we got the opportunity to spend some seat time with the updated cars.

articles.headline: Hull should be in League One, says xG - so how do they keep winning?
keyFacts: Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table, despite Expected Goals data indicating they should be in League One.
Manager Sergej Jakirovic stated that Hull focus on moving the ball quickly and being efficient in attack despite having the lowest possession in the league.
Hull rely on a selective press, strong performances from goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, and opponent misses to secure results.
body: Hull City should be in League One this season according to Expected Goals - so how do the Tigers keep winning in the Premier League?

Hull City are sitting comfortably in the middle of the Premier League table - when the Expected Goals underlying data says they should be two divisions below; watch Crystal Palace vs Hull live on Sky Sports this Sunday from 1pm, kick-off 2pm
Thursday 26 November 2026 14:53, UK
Hull aren't doing much wrong as a newly promoted club so far. A great start to the campaign has them middle of the Premier League table, clear of the relegation zone and unbeaten at home all season.
These are all the right ingredients for survival. But the underlying data says otherwise.

If Expected Goals (xG) decided football matches - yes, yes, we know they don't - then Hull would be bottom of the Premier League, with a similar record to the actual bottom club Crystal Palace, who they play live on Sky Sports this Sunday.

The reason? Hull have only won one game this season on xG since their promotion to the top flight.On its own, this underlying data should be taken with a pinch of salt. xG numbers in a match require context.
For example, a team that loses a game can often end up having a higher xG than the opponent, as they were chasing the game and attacking for longer periods.

- Got Sky? Watch Premier League games LIVE on your phone📱
- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream PL games with no contract📺

The same xG table also has Chelsea in 14th place at the moment. Bournemouth should be third and Nottingham Forest should be sixth. After 11 games, there is a lot of differentiation between the Expected Table and the actual table across the board.
But this isn't a new phenomenon when it comes to Hull. The fascinating thing about the Tigers is that this has been happening for 18 months.

The same xG data says Hull should also be playing in League One this season. That's because last term, they should have finished second-bottom of the Championship after 46 games, according to xG. Instead, they were promoted to the Premier League via the play-offs.
As Aston Villa showed last season, you can get away with overperforming this way for some time but things eventually regress to the mean. To do this over a long period of time is extraordinary.
So why are Hull where they are? Style has something to do with it.

Set up in a 5-4-1 formation, Hull have the lowest possession in the Premier League this season by an absolute country mile. The same applies for the number of shots they have and how high they start pressing up the pitch.

"It is not about possession, it is what you do with it," said manager Sergej Jakirovic told Sky Sports in an interview last month. Hull are comfortable in a low block, which ultimately leads to losing the 'stats side' of games.
So how do Hull actually win games? As their manager says, in the little time Hull get hold of the ball, they use it to good effect - the Tigers move the ball up the pitch quicker than any other team.

There is also an efficiency in attack. In the Championship last season, Hull had two of the most clinical forwards in Ollie McBurnie and Joe Gelhardt. They were given few opportunities, but when they got them, they took them.
The same culture applies here. "No matter who is the opponent, we will have our chances," added Jakirovic.
The aim of the game is not only to progress the ball as quickly as possible, but also choosing the right battles. That can be seen in Hull's pressing.

Hull barely press - they have the lowest number of high turnovers in the Premier League this season. However, they have the second-most goals from high turnovers this season and rank fourth for high pressures that end up in a shot. It's a selective, patient press.

Take their recent draw with Brentford as an example. Their only chance of the first half came from Hull pressing out-of-position midfielder Aaron Hickey to win a penalty which they scored from. Then they relied on the defence to hold out for a result. They conceded late, but got what many would say is a good point.

But this game plan of little possession and reliance on taking advantage of the few attacks that come their way is risky. You need a lot of luck to go your way, and Hull have had their fair share of that.
In the Championship last season, Hull had the most let-offs out of any second-tier team in terms of big chances missed by their opponents. A similar theme has continued in the Premier League.

In Hull's first two home games of the season, Man Utd and Aston Villa should have scored around two goals each, according to xG. Neither of those teams found the net, as the Tigers picked up four points instead.
But it is not just luck. In their most recent home game against Brighton, the performance of Konstantinos Tzolakis caught the eye, which confirms skills matters as well.

The Greek goalkeeper - or 'Greek God' as many Hull fans were claiming last weekend - has the best save record out of any Premier League goalkeeper this season. He alone has prevented nearly 2.0 worth of xG going in.

Without him, and without the game plan from their experienced manager, Hull would be closer to the bottom of the table. Instead, they go to the Premier League's basement club knowing they can still get a result.

articles.headline: New Zealand election results set up tricky talks for conservative incumbent
keyFacts: Final New Zealand election results showed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's ruling coalition fell one seat short of a parliamentary majority.
Qiulae Wong's Opportunity Party won seven seats, positioning her centrist party as a kingmaker for coalition negotiations.
Political scientist Luke Oldfield said a right-bloc deal is likely, though failure to reach an agreement could trigger another election.
body: The final results of New Zealand’s November 7 election offer no clear path to forming a government, suggesting tricky political wrangling is likely in the weeks ahead.

The results, released on Friday, showed that the ruling centre-right coalition led by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s conservative National Party has fallen one seat short of a parliamentary majority.

Luxon has led New Zealand since 2023, but National and its junior partners – the populist New Zealand First and libertarian ACT – won just 65 seats between them. National secured 40 seats while ACT and New Zealand First won 13 seats and 12 seats, respectively.
The result reflects a loss of support for Luxon driven by a stagnant economy, and leaves the former businessman and his coalition partners to seek additional help to secure a majority.
“New Zealanders need a government that is stable, that works together and will last for the full term,” Luxon told a news conference on Friday.
Labour, the largest opposition party, won 36 seats, leaving it far below the 66-seat threshold in the 130-member parliament.
The results appear to position Qiulae Wong’s centrist Opportunity Party, which clinched 7 seats, as kingmaker. However, talks with the conservative and populist incumbents are likely to prove tricky.
The former consultant has promised a universal basic income of up to NZ$370 (US$208) a week, greater action on climate change, a ban on bottom-trawling fishing, and healthcare reforms.
She has also campaigned for a kinder approach to politics. Wong has pledged to do “everything we can” to ensure a stable government.

Her style contrasts with that of potential suitors such as Winston Peters of New Zealand First. The controversial foreign minister has called opponents “morons” and drew shock earlier this year when he told a Chinese-born lawmaker to “go back to your country”. His party promises to tighten immigration flows and withdraw from the Paris Climate Accord.
Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour of ACT campaigned against a greater governance role for the Indigenous Maori minority and has promised massive cuts to state spending.
Failure to meet an agreement could see Kiwis return to the polls next year.
Luke Oldfield, a political scientist at Victoria University of Wellington, told Reuters news agency a deal was likely, although it could be challenging.
“I don’t know exactly what kind of shape that will be yet, but it’ll be highly likely that there will be a right bloc formed and not a second election,” he said.

articles.headline: Australia's sandpapergate probe to also include 2017-18 Ashes
keyFacts: Cricket Australia expanded its independent probe into the sandpapergate scandal to include the 2017-18 Ashes series.
Cricket Australia stated that participants are not compelled to speak and will face no retrospective sanctions.
Cricket Australia pledged to publish the full independent report and its recommendations within 30 days of receipt.
body: - Published
Cricket Australia's fresh independent probe into the sandpapergate scandal has been widened to include the 2017-18 Ashes series against England.

The terms of reference for the independent forum have been published and the scope will include "ball-management practices in the Australian men's team during the 2017â18 season", which includes the Ashes series Australia won 4-0.
Also included are all four Tests of the subsequent South Africa tour and the investigation which followed when the ball-tampering scandal emerged.
Cricket Australia has pledged to publish the full independent report and recommendations within 30 days of receiving them.
All those involved in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa will be invited to speak to the independent forum, though none will have to do so and no retrospective sanctions will be handed out.

The scandal was reignited by the release of former batter Usman Khawaja's autobiography. In it, Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about ball-tampering in the third Test of their series against South Africa in Cape Town.

The four frontline bowlers in that 2018 team - Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc, Nathan Lyon and current Test captain Pat Cummins - have always denied knowledge of the plan to use sandpaper on the ball.
Cummins has called Khawaja's recollection of events "nonsense".
However, former team-mates David Warner and Cameron Bancroft - two of three players who were banned for their part in the scandal, alongside Steve Smith - have backed Khawaja's version of events.

"All participants in Australia's 2018 tour of South Africa, including players and support staff, will be invited to take part in the Independent Forum, as will CA management and directors at that time," Cricket Australia said.

"While all involved will be encouraged to participate, there will be no compulsion to do so. All materials supplied will be treated as confidential unless otherwise stated by the participant and no sanctions will be retrospectively applied.
"Participants can choose to attend the Independent Forum in person, online and/or provide information via written accounts or through relevant documents and materials."
The forum will be open for six weeks.

"This is an opportunity to provide their accounts in a safe environment and to provide the CA Board with relevant information including about the events of that tour and resultant investigation," CA chair David Boon said.
"We are acutely aware of the enormous toll the renewed focus on this tour eight years ago has had on those involved and their welfare remains our main priority.
"This forum is the best opportunity for people to speak and be heard, and for CA to listen and learn.
"Publishing the report in full is part of our commitment to transparency, and to be open with cricket fans about what we learn.
"It is also very important to understand that it will not seek to sanction or recriminate."

Writing in his autobiography in 2019, former England opener Sir Alastair Cook - who captained England in the 2017-18 Ashes - alleged Warner admitted during post-series drinks that he had previously used strapping on his finger to tamper with the ball.
The final Ashes Test in Sydney was just two months before the start of the South Africa series.
"Our suspicions had been aroused in Perth, when they managed to get the ball reversing an inordinate amount when the outfield was still wet, following three hours' rain," Cook wrote.
"When the series was complete, and we had lost 4-0, the teams shared a beer in the dressing rooms at the SCG.

"Warner, a couple of beers into his celebration at the time, mentioned to a group of England players that he had used substances attached to the strapping on his hand to accelerate the deterioration of the ball during a first-class match.
"I looked at Steve Smith, who shot a glance that said 'ooh, you shouldn't have said that'."

articles.headline: Support team put in an emergency order for vodka – lots of vodka – to bring PCs back online
keyFacts: A flooded computer room knocked out ancient PCs powering a global radio station, according to a tech support worker named Bruce.
Support staff cleaned the drenched computer parts with isopropanol and an emergency delivery of vodka before drying them outside.
The team rebuilt the PCs after discovering a new facilities hire accidentally released stagnant tank water into the room, Bruce said.
body: The end of the working week is often enough to drive tech support people to drink, which is why The Register likes to get the party started early. Friday mornings bring a new installment of On Call – the column in which we share your stories of doing whatever it takes to keep tech running.
This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Bruce," who told us that in the mid-2000s he worked for a global radio station.
"We used to have about 30 PCs, all running slightly different radio shows depending on the time zone where we broadcast," he explained.
The PCs were old clunkers running Windows 95 long after Microsoft ended support for the OS. Management knew the machines needed replacing, but funding was probably another year away.
"We had to coax them on till then," Bruce wrote. "And by coax, I mean we were buying RAM on eBay because nobody sold the 4MB sticks we needed anymore."
Thanks to the tender ministrations of Bruce and his colleagues, the PCs kept humming and the radio stations stayed on the air.
Until a lovely spring Tuesday, when Bruce and his crew enjoyed a bucolic cup of tea in the first real sunshine of the season and received a call informing them that one of the stations was down.
One of Bruce's mates figured a cranky old PC probably just needed a reboot and headed off to fix it while the rest of the team enjoyed their tea.
And then the phone rang again to report another outage, so Bruce and the entire crew went back to work, chatting about which switch or other shared device could have taken out two PCs.
When they arrived in the office, the chap who had gone to reboot the first PC ran in and announced that the computer room had flooded.
Bruce and his teammates ran into that room and found dirty brown water all over the floor, walls, ceiling, and the racks holding the ancient PCs.
"Water was even spraying out of the front fans of the last two PCs that were still working," Bruce told The Register .

"After a lot of shouting words unfit to print, we all got to work ripping them out, shutting down what we could that looked to be working, and started lining them up outside in the car park," Bruce wrote. "Some of us then got to work stripping them down into component parts, others washed them down with isopropanol."
As the isopropanol supply dwindled, one of the team arranged an urgent delivery of vodka.
"Luckily, it was a gloriously sunny day, so we quickly rinsed the PCs and left them to dry, strewn all over the car park," Bruce wrote.
By this stage, he and the team were all filthy and exhausted. With the stations still offline, they had to rebuild the PCs and get them running again.
"We only lost two sticks of RAM, one sound card, and a power supply," Bruce wrote.
The culprit turned out to be a new hire on the facilities team who, while touring the building, had turned a random tap to see what would happen.

"It released water from a stagnant iron tank that sat there rusting away for years," Bruce wrote. For reasons nobody understood, the tank drained through a pipe into the room housing the broadcast PCs.

Have you had to clean up hardware in a hurry, perhaps with odd substances or implements? If so, click here to send On Call your story. We'll raise a glass to each one of you who sends a story and do it again if we share it on a future Friday. ®

articles.headline: India's Modi government calls special sitting of parliament
keyFacts: India's government called a special parliament sitting, with the Lok Sabha meeting Monday and the Rajya Sabha meeting Wednesday.
Congress General Secretary Jairam Ramesh called the sitting an assault on India's Constitution and accused the government of manufacturing a fraudulent majority.
The Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group plans to meet Saturday, while official memos indicate the session may conclude on December 3.
body: What you need to know
These are our rolling updates from India on Friday, November 27:
- A brief sitting of the Indian parliament will take place after the monsoon session was adjourned indefinitely back in August
- India's Lok Sabha is set to meet on Monday
- The Rajya Sabha will resume proceedings on Wednesday
How has india's opposition reacted to the reconvening of parliament?

India's main opposition Congress party has deemed the move by Modi's government to call for the brief sitting of the parliament "an assault on the Constitution of India" which Congress General Secretary in-charge Communications and MP Jairam Ramesh said "must and will be resisted with all might."
In a post on X, Ramesh accused the government of "moving to manufacture a fraudulent two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha"
Ramesh also listed out a three-point Congress stance on delimitation and women's quota, which includes:
- Maintaining the current strength of the Lok Sabha for another 25 years.
- Maintaining the current state-wise distribution of seats in the Lok Sabha for another 25 years
- Implementation of one-third reservation for women and reservation within reservation for women belonging to Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes from the next general elections, slated for 2029.
A meeting of the Congress Parliamentary Strategy Group is also expected to be held on Saturday to discuss the gameplan for the upcoming parliament sitting, news agency ANI reported.
Indian parliament to hold special sitting after a gap of more than 100 days

A political storm could be on the horizon in India as both houses of India's bicameral parliament are set to reconvene next week for a special sitting at the request of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.
The Lok Sabha (lower house) is slated to sit on November 30 while the Rajya Sabha (upper house) will meet on December 2, official memos said, adding that the session may conclude on December 3.

"The Government has requested Hon'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha and Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha to reconvene Lok Sabha on Monday, 30th November, 2026 and Rajya Sabha on Wednesday, 2nd December, 2026 respectively to transact essential Government Business," Union Minister of Parliamentary Affairs Kiren Rijiju wrote on X, announcing the government's request on Thursday evening.

The resumption of parliament comes after the monsoon session, which is the second regular session of India's legislative body, saw both the houses being adjourned sine die (indefinitely) on August 13.
The session never ended formally and has remained unprorogued for a record over 100 days, while a winter session that typically starts early December looks delayed.

The monsoon session was turbulent as it began amid a massive youth-led protest called by India's "Cockroach" movement that sought, and later managed to get, the resignation of Modi's then-education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities.

The parliament, itself, became a protest ground as both Modi's ruling coalition, led by his Bharatiya Janata Party, and the opposition INDIA bloc, by Congress, held demonstrations within its premises.
The political deadlock was unrelenting and the parliament struggled to get much business underway, culminating in the adjournment.
Welcome to our coverage
This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's bureau in New Delhi, back with your daily dose of news from India.
Here is what's creating a buzz in the world's largest democracy this morning:

Indian lawmakers are making their way back to the parliament next week, more than three months after a rocky — and not formal — conclusion of the monsoon session of the country's supreme legislative body which struggled to conduct its business amid an outpouring of protests against Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over student issues.

The Modi government's request to reconvene both houses of the parliament for a special sitting has been accepted, with parliamentarians huddling in the Lok Sabha — the lower house — on November 30 and Rajya Sabha — the upper house — on December 2.
The ruling coalition has not explicitly stated what affairs it wants to discuss during the short session and has only said it wants to "transact essential government business."

However, speculation is rife that Modi's government could once again push a package of defeated bills — including a contentious population-based redrawing of voting boundaries and a women's quota intertwined with it.

And in the world of cricket, it is day one of the second test match between India and New Zealand in Christchurch's Hagley Oval . Both teams are vying for a series win in this final match after the first one in Wellington ended in a draw.

articles.headline: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
keyFacts: Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Time reporter, died Thursday at age 80, his son confirmed.
Under President Bill Clinton, Talbott served as deputy secretary of state and shaped U.S. policy toward Russia.
Talbott later served as president of the Brookings Institution from 2002 to 2017 and authored over a dozen books.
body: Strobe Talbott, former Time magazine reporter and deputy secretary of state, has died
Strobe Talbott, a former Time magazine reporter who later served as deputy secretary of state under President Bill Clinton and then headed the Brookings Institution, died Thursday. He was 80.
His son, Devin Talbott, confirmed he passed away peacefully after a long illness in his East Hampton, New York, home.

The elder Talbott was educated at Yale and Oxford, where he bunked with Clinton. While at the British university, after interning for Time in Moscow, the magazine asked Talbott to help translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former first secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union who was ousted in 1964.
Talbott did, and it gave him some notoriety as a young man and a job at the magazine.

After 21 years at Time, where he focused on Soviet-American relations and held positions including Washington bureau chief and a foreign-affairs columnist, according to his U.S. State Department biography, he received a call from the newly elected Clinton.

Talbott joined the U.S. State Department in 1994, swiftly becoming deputy secretary of state. In that role, he was the architect of the Clinton administration's approach to Russia and other formerly Soviet countries and conducted negotiations between the U.S. and India after the latter's nuclear tests in 1998.

"Strobe was a good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," said Clinton in a statement after Talbott's death. When Talbott was translating Khrushchev's memoirs while at Oxford, it was Clinton's job to make him breakfast every day, he said, adding, "somehow, I got the better end of the deal."
Both he and Hillary were "deeply saddened" by the passing of "a wonderful friend, and a world-class human being," he said.
Afterward, he served as the president of Brookings from 2002 to 2017. In that time, he also chaired the U.S. State Department's Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Talbott also authored over a dozen books. His last book was titled "Our Founders' Warning: The Age of Reason Meets the Age of Trump," which was published in 2020.
He was born in Dayton, Ohio, in 1946, and is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren.
His first wife, Brook Shearer, died in 2009, and he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.

body: - Published
A massive Thanksgiving storm hammering the Midwest and north-east with heavy rain and winds, along with high tides out west, is causing widespread disruptions across the US.

More than 80 million Americans expected to be travelling this week. On Thursday 460 flights in the US were cancelled and another 2,508 flights into, out of, or within the US were delayed, tracking site FlightAware said.
The FAA has previously warned that delays would be possible "throughout the week" as a result of the rain and wind that are forecast.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul also declared a state of emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County.
In New York City, organisers of the annual Macy's Thanksgiving parade have postponed the event to Saturday.
Bridges closed in Maryland due to severe winds and waves battered beaches in Delaware as water seeped onto the boardwalk.
In Maryland, almost two million customers have been asked by the water utility to use water for essential use only due to "intermittent power disruptions".
On the wettest Thanksgiving on record in Washington DC, tidal waters surged and soaked runways at Reagan Washington National Airport, according to the National Water Prediction Service.
More than 980,000 households were reporting power outages by Thursday evening, with Pennsylvania, Virginia, Maryland and New Jersey hit particularly hard.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro said that utility providers were working tirelessly to restore power. Meanwhile, energy companies in Virginia and New Jersey warned it may take some time, even days, for power to return, as crews had to wait until it was safe to access damaged areas.
On Thursday afternoon, President Donald Trump said he would consider releasing emergency funds for the east coast as it faces down the holiday storm.
Across the US, severe weather is also descending on the West Coast. The NWS has warned of a series of Pacific storms that are expected to bring rain, mountain snow and strong winds.
Many are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak along the coast.
Water levels along California's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Thursday, according to the NWS, breaking records set just last month.
Both San Diego and Los Angeles reported a high tide of over 8ft earlier in the week, and beach-goers were advised to avoid coastal areas.
Train services along the Amtrak Pacific Surfliner, which runs along the California coastline, cancelled several trains due to "washout conditions from high tides", the company shared on social media.
Storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia.
In Miami, some travel delays persisted into Thursday after a FedEx plane overshot the runway the night before, which prompted the closure of all but one runway at the airport for a brief period.
A statement FedEx provided to US media confirmed that one of its flights had "experienced an issue upon landing".

It added: "We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA."
An airport employee who spoke anonymously to CBS News, the BBC's US partner, raised the possibility that rainy conditions had been a factor.

"They tried as hard as they could to stop, but I don't know if it was the weather because the rain and the wind were really bad, and they just couldn't stop in time and went right off the runway and veered off into the grass," they said.
Wednesday's incident in Miami came 11 weeks after a cargo plane crashed on landing at the same airport, killing five people and injuring five others in vehicles on the ground with which it collided.
The American Automobile Association (AAA) predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for the Thanksgiving holiday over a seven-day period.
Rebecka Pieder contributed reporting.

articles.headline: NFL Week 12 grades for Thanksgiving: Cowboys choke their way to a 'D,' Bears earn 'B' for big win
keyFacts: The NFL held its first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game on Wednesday night, with the Rams defeating the Packers 26-13.
All three Thanksgiving Day matchups were decided by a game-winning score in the final five seconds, marking a first in NFL history.
The Eagles defeated the Cowboys 39-38 after overcoming a 31-10 deficit, setting a record for the largest blown lead on Thanksgiving.
body: Welcome to the Turkey edition of the Week 12 grades!
Playing on Thanksgiving is one of the NFL's longest running traditions, but this year, it's not just about Thanksgiving. The league is trying to take over nearly the entire week.

The holiday slate of games kicked off on Wednesday night with the Rams beating the Packers 26-13 in the NFL's first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game. Hopefully you enjoyed the NFL's newest tradition, because it will be sticking around. The league is planning .

The game between the Rams and Packers served as the appetizer for possibly the craziest Thanksgiving slate ever. All three matchups were decided by a game-winning score in the final five seconds, marking the first time that's every happened on Thanksgiving in NFL history.

The Turkey Day action started in Detroit, where the Bears pulled off a dramatic 39-35 win in a game where Caleb Williams threw a touchdown pass to Rome Odunze with just three seconds left to help Chicago stun Detroit. The two teams combined for 1,007 yards of offense, which is the second-most ever in a Thanksgiving game.

The game in Detroit was crazy, but the second game of the day in Dallas might have topped it, with the Cowboys blowing a 31-10 lead in a 39-38 loss to the Eagles. It was the largest blown lead on Thanksgiving in NFL history. It also made the Cowboys the first team in NFL history to blow a lead of 14 points or more in the fourth quarter TWICE at home in a single season.

The Turkey Day nightcap took place in Buffalo, where the weather shut down the offensive shootout that we were all expecting to see. With temperatures under 40 degrees and a steady rain falling for the entire game, the Josh Allen vs. Patrick Mahomes showdown turned into a defensive struggle with the Bills coming out on top in a 13-10 thriller. The Bills might want to ask the NFL if they can play on Thanksgiving every year, because Josh Allen is now 4-0 on the holiday.
There will be one more game coming on Friday (Broncos at Steelers), but before we get to that, let's hand out some grades for the four games that have been played so far.

articles.headline: Stephen King's Psychological Thriller Officially Says Goodbye to Streaming
keyFacts: Brian De Palma’s 1976 film adaptation of Stephen King’s novel Carrie will leave HBO Max on November 30.
The story follows an abused teenager who discovers she has telekinetic powers and unleashes violence after being humiliated at her prom.
Stephen King praised the film adaptation, specifically complimenting the performances of Sissy Spacek and John Travolta.
body: Stephen King’s books have inspired countless adaptations over the years. Several have even been adapted for the screen more than once, including Firestarter (1984 and 2022) and The Running Man (1987 and 2025).

However, one film adaptation stands out for its distinctive impact on the horror genre. That film is Brian De Palma’s 1976 supernatural horror classic, Carrie, featuring Sissy Spacek as our titular protagonist. And while its story has been adapted multiple times in both film and TV, the original remains unbeatable.

With Carrie leaving HBO Max on Nov. 30, there's never been a better time to hide from your family this Thanksgiving and spend the afternoon watching a young woman pushed to the brink and unleashing supernatural violence.
What is Carrie about?

King's story follows awkward 16-year-old Carrie White as she faces torment at home and at school. At home, her abusive mother’s religious fanaticism creates an oppressive environment. At school, a group of popular girls targets her. When Carrie gets her first period, her main bully, Chris (Nancy Allen), cruelly humiliates her and encourages the girls to pelt her with tampons. Carrie’s teacher, Miss Collins (Betty Buckley), punishes Chris and bars her from attending prom. Furious, Chris begins plotting revenge against Carrie.

However, Carrie’s discovery comes with a frightening catch: Whenever she becomes upset, she can move objects with her mind. As she struggles to understand and control this mysterious ability, Chris carries out her plan to humiliate Carrie in front of everyone at prom. The two events collide, turning the night into a bloodbath as Carrie unleashes an unprecedented wave of vengeance against her tormentors, including her mother.
What does King think of De Palma’s Carrie?

Over the years, Stephen King has never hesitated to speak out about adaptations of his books that, in his view, stray from the original meaning. One well-known example is Stanley Kubrick’s The Shining, which King fans know he has criticized so harshly that he once described the film as “a big, beautiful Cadillac with no engine inside it.”
King feels quite differently about De Palma’s Carrie. In an interview with Cinefantastique, he praised De Palma’s take on his book, even though the film is far more satirical than the novel.

“Sissy Spacek was excellent, but right behind her — in a smaller part than it should have been — was John Travolta,” King said. “He played the part of Billy Nolan the way I wish I’d written it, half-funny and half-crazy.”
What makes De Palma’s Carrie so timeless?

Over the years, King’s Carrie has been adapted in many ways, though not all for film. The latest adaptation is by Mike Flanagan, known for Midnight Mass, and has generally been well received, with an 85% Tomatometer score on Rotten Tomatoes.

Yet, as beloved as Flanagan’s adaptation is, horror fans owe it to themselves to watch the classic that launched the Carrie franchise. For one thing, King was absolutely right to praise Spacek, who captures Carrie’s vulnerability with heartbreaking precision while also conveying her rage through subtle yet striking physical gestures. Even a single twitch of her eye makes you stand up straight, waiting for her to snap.

More importantly, as the first screen adaptation of King’s work to achieve both critical and commercial success (it earned $33.8 million at the box office on a modest $1.8 million budget), Carrie undoubtedly helped make King a household name in horror. It showed that his work could translate well to the big screen and paved the way for later cinematic classics like The Shining, Cujo, and Christine.
With such monumental success behind it, the only question we’ve got is this: Why aren’t you watching Carrie right now? Go on, git.
Carrie is available to watch now exclusively on HBO Max. But don’t wait too long; it leaves the streamer on Nov. 30.

articles.headline: Witcher 3 Remastered patch has lighting fixes, sign nerfs, and gets rid of a nasty werewolf bug
keyFacts: Developers released patch 5.02 for The Witcher 3 Remastered to fix a bug where werewolves regenerated health too quickly on higher difficulties.
The patch addresses various lighting issues and includes optimizations for Path Tracing, Ray Reconstruction, and hair rendering.
Developers implemented balance changes and skill nerfs, including a reduction to the Catalyst skill's bonus and stamina regeneration.
body: If you replayed The Witcher 3 in its shiny new remastered form and got absolutely bodied by a couple of werewolf fights you thought were easier back when you had more youthful reflexes, don't worry—the problem wasn't your aging brain and hands after all. It was a bug that's been caught and exterminated in patch 5.02. "Fixed an issue where werewolves could regenerate health too quickly on higher difficulty settings," the patch notes say, "making them impossible to defeat."

Another problem some players had with The Witcher 3 Remastered was its lighting, with interiors in particular looking too dark while some other locations were washed-out flashbangs. Good news: "Fixed various lighting issues across multiple locations and cutscenes," the patch notes say, "including overly bright or dark areas, inconsistent lighting transitions and flickering." They've also "Fixed various lighting issues with hair when Path Tracing is enabled" and "Made various Path Tracing and Ray Reconstruction optimizations and visual improvements, including lighting, shadows, and water rendering."

That's all positive stuff, but the balance changes to various signs and mutations will be more controversial. The Remastered version launched with buffs to Witcher signs that made them useful even if you didn't specialize in them, but it may have overdone things a little. This patch walks back some of the potential for you to dominate the entire game with an Aard build, though changes like reducing the Catalyst skill's bonus to Aard and Igni intensity by 10% don't seem like they'll totally change the way you play.

I get that people don't like skill nerfs in singleplayer games, but I can also see CD Projekt anticipating next year's Songs of the Past DLC. They don't want to hear a bunch of players say, "It sucked because I trivialized the whole thing with a broken build I got by copying a YouTuber." If some skill nerfs and a reduction to stamina regeneration in combat mean you have to drink more potions to get your signs off, it probably won't ruin your fun.

Oh, and if you couldn't complete your Gwent collection because Zoltan Chivay's card didn't show up, the patch notes say it'll now appear in the correct place under the Hanged Man's Tree in Velen. Time to go back and get that 100% achievement at last.

Jody's first computer was a Commodore 64, so he remembers having to use a code wheel to play Pool of Radiance. articles.headline: Nearly 900,000 customers without power as of Thanksgiving evening
keyFacts: East Coast storms left nearly 900,000 U.S. customers without power as of Thanksgiving evening, according to Poweroutage.us.
Severe weather delayed or canceled thousands of flights and forced the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to be postponed to Saturday.
WSSC Water asked nearly two million Maryland residents to conserve water after storms affected local water filtration plants.
body: Storms ravaging the East Coast put around 900,000 customers in the United States out of power as of Thanksgiving evening.

Poweroutage.us , a U.S. power outage monitor, listed the worst outages in Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, New Jersey, and Washington, D.C. Tens of thousands more in Missouri, Connecticut, New York, North Carolina, and Delaware were also left without power.

Pennsylvania and New Jersey both saw outages reach nearly 200,000 on Thursday evening. Missouri saw tens of thousands of people without power due to severe snowstorms Wednesday night and into Thursday.
The inclement weather threw a wrench in Thanksgiving plans across the country. The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed to Saturday, the first time in its history the event was moved.

Flights were similarly affected. Tracking website FlightAware noted 2,461 flights within, into, or out of the United States were delayed, while 459 were canceled. The day before, over 7,200 were delayed and 168 canceled. A handful of airports, such as LaGuardia in New York and Reagan National Airport in Washington, experienced temporary ground stops due to the weather.
Storms and flooding caused property damage across the East Coast as well, including homes and cars damaged by falling trees and branches, with some areas eclipsing 4 inches of rainfall.

Some areas were able to improve as time progressed throughout Thursday. Dominion Energy said the number of customers without power in Virginia went from around 141,000 at 4:30 p.m. to 115,500 at 7:45 p.m.
PRINCE GEORGE’S AND MONTGOMERY COUNTIES ASKED TO CONSERVE WATER AMID THANKSGIVING STORMS

But the effects of the power outages had cascading effects that affected millions more people across the East Coast. Nearly 2 million residents in the Maryland suburbs of Washington, D.C. , were asked to conserve water after storms put one water filtration plant out of power and another one in a state of uncertainty.

Residents in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were told by WSSC Water to limit showers, flushing, use of dishwashers and washing machines, and other appliance use on Thanksgiving to conserve water.

articles.headline: Strobe Talbott, former deputy secretary of state and Brookings Institution president, dies at 80
keyFacts: Former Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott died Thursday at age 80 after a long illness, his son said.
Talbott worked at Time magazine before serving as deputy secretary of state and leading the Brookings Institution.
Former President Bill Clinton said Talbott helped build trust with Russia, reduce nuclear dangers, and expand NATO.
body: Strobe Talbott, a former deputy secretary of state whose deep expertise on the Soviet Union shaped U.S. foreign policy before he went on to lead the Brookings Institution, died Thursday at the age of 80.
Talbott’s son, Devin Talbott, said his father died peacefully after a long illness at his home in East Hampton, New York, The Associated Press reported.

An Ohio native, Talbott began his journalism career as an intern at Time magazine while studying at Yale and Oxford, where he was roommates with future President Bill Clinton . Clinton later joked that his job in their shared apartment was to make Talbott breakfast every morning.
NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL
While at Time, Talbott was tapped to translate the leaked memoirs of Nikita Khrushchev, the former Soviet leader ousted in 1964, which earned him a full-time role at the magazine.
Over a 21-year career there, he focused on U.S.-Soviet relations, led the Washington bureau, and wrote as a foreign affairs columnist.
In 1994, Talbott joined the Clinton administration as deputy secretary of state, helping guide U.S. relations with Russia and other post-Soviet states.
In a statement, Bill Clinton said no one was better suited to advise him on Russian affairs than Talbott, noting that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton also relied on his counsel.
TRUMP PUSHED NATO TO SPEND BIG — NOW COMES THE HARDER QUESTION: CAN EUROPE ACTUALLY FIGHT?

"He was analytical, completely devoted to diplomacy, and on the level," Bill Clinton said. "With his expertise, we made real progress building trust between two former adversaries — moving beyond decades of confrontation to reduce the nuclear dangers future generations would inherit and build a Europe where more people could live in freedom and peace, including through the expansion of NATO and resolving ethnic conflicts in the Balkans. Together we laid the groundwork for greater cooperation while putting Russia on a path to democracy."
"Sadly, its current leader has taken the country in a different direction," Clinton added, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin .
He described Talbott as a "good and brilliant man who made our world more peaceful and secure," and said, "Hillary and I will miss him very much."
After leaving government, Talbott served as president of the Brookings Institution from 2002 to 2017 and chaired the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
He is survived by two sons, Devin and Adrian, and six grandchildren. His first wife, Brooke Shearer, died in 2009; he later married author Barbara Lazear Ascher.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
