articles.headline: Why is there a shortage of 'wizard' elevator mechanics?
keyFacts: A shortage of elevator mechanics is worsening in the US and UK despite average US salaries of $110,000, industry figures say.
The labor shortage delays elevator repairs, stranding residents such as the elderly and wheelchair users who rely on lifts.
Industry experts suggest teaching trade basics in high schools and offering tax breaks to help attract new mechanics.
body: - Published
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.
"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."
Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them â elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped, external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.
In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic, external is $110,000 (Â£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height â or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."
Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.
"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.
"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.
But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.
Hollinshead says teaching the basics of the trade in high schools or technical schools could entice more people into the role.

Matt Allred, a recruiter and host of The Elevator Careers Podcast, emphasises the many skills that lift mechanics require. "You're a little bit of a wizard, right? You show up and if you can fix it â 'Wow!'."
He blames major lift companies, in part, for locking down maintenance contracts, making it difficult or impossible for third-party repairers to intervene when a lift fails.

Two large lift manufacturers approached by BBC News declined interviews. The chief executive of Otis, one of the firms, said in May that her company was struggling to hire enough staff, external to meet demand. The firm also states on its website, external that the shortage of lift mechanics affects "almost every part of the world".
However, a spokesman for Otis claimed its "US talent pipeline" was healthy, and declined an interview.

Everyone else who spoke to BBC News said hiring was challenging in the US. Allred was recently contacted by a major lift company and asked to help them find a technician. "I was surprised that a major company would reach out to a little recruiting shop," he says, suggesting that this reflects the extent of the labour shortage.

That shortage is also a problem in the UK. "It is bad and getting worse," says Dave Cooper, president of the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers, who is also chief executive of a lift and escalator engineering consultancy.
"We've known food delivery companies to refuse to deliver to flats above the ground floor because the lift is out of service."
Offering better tax breaks to companies that train lift mechanics could help ensure that plenty of workers continue to enter the industry, he adds.

Training to be a lift mechanic is "not a quick route to competency â and it requires people to stick at it for the long term" says Karen Slade, head of assessment at the Lift and Escalator Industry Association (Leia).
Continued investment in training and attracting new workers is "essential", according to Leia. There are currently 259 active lift and escalator apprentices in the UK, the body adds.
Back in Chicago, Lembesis is working with two younger mechanics who have been "really good", he says, so there's at least some hope for the future.
He stresses again how rewarding he finds his work. The people for whom he fixes lifts tend to be very appreciative.
"I love that. You get that reaction from the customers," he says. "Without them, you got nothing."

articles.headline: Dark fantasy and sudoku fuse together in unholy matrimony in Dungoku, a dungeon crawling twist on the classic puzzle game
keyFacts: Dungoku is a newly announced genre mashup combining dungeon crawling and sudoku with a retro dark fantasy theme.
Players place enemies and chests on grid-based maps according to specific placement rules, while acquiring loot and avoiding damage from mistakes.
The game features over 100 dungeons and more than 20 monsters, with no release date currently announced.
body: Maths is not my strong suit, I make no secret of this, so when I come face to face with something like sudoku I will admit to recoiling in fear at having to confront this issue. Numbers don't make sense to me at the best of times, and now I have to figure out the specific placements of them whereby each number can only be used once per section, and each column and row have to all contain numbers one through nine? Terrifying! No, thanks, I'd much rather do the exact same thing but with, I don't know, skeletons and ghouls and the like. Which, conveniently, is more or less what Dungoku offers, a genre mashup of dungeon crawling and sudoku with a retro dark fantasy vibe.

Okay, it's not exactly the same. You don't crawl the dungeons in the typical fashion here as it leans heavily towards the puzzle side of things. Maps come in different, grid-based shapes and sizes, but to start they are mostly void of enemies. It's predominantly up to you to place enemies, or sometimes chests, in specific squares, all of which have their own rules that you must follow, with a set number that need to be placed on the map.

For example, one enemy may have a requirement that it is adjacent to a zombie in the same room. Another might need to be placed in a dead end. Others, like an owl creature, can only share a room with itself or other animals. So, it's different from sudoku in that each puzzle features changing enemies that have to be placed, as opposed to always needing to follow the same basic rules. It seems like a clever spin on the classic puzzle! Plus there's loot to be acquired that improves your stats and thereby your chance of survival (making a mistake in placement results in, obviously, getting hurt; this is still a dungeon crawler!).

In total there's apparently over 100 "hand-crafted dungeons to explore," and more than 20 monsters to take on, so it sounds like there's some good potential for interesting puzzle combinations. I also like the specific mention of "human composed music," certainly makes it sound like AI wasn't involved, and lord almighty I hope that to be true! No release date attached to this one just yet, but you can wishlist it on Steam in the meantime.

articles.headline: Nearly Three Decades And Four Consoles Later, I Finally Beat Ocarina Of Time
keyFacts: A GameSpot writer finally beat The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time twenty-eight years after first playing it as a child.
The writer previously struggled to finish the game across multiple consoles including the Nintendo 64, GameCube, and 3DS.
A new remake of the game on Nintendo Switch 2 helped the writer stay engaged until reaching the final battle.
body: I finally did it.

As Princess Zelda held the transformed, monstrous Ganon in place with her magic, I delivered the final blow with the Master Sword. The Demon King was sealed away and Hyrule was saved. I found myself getting emotional, because this was the first time in 28 years that I had beaten The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

For many, that would mean it was also the first time they had played Ocarina of Time, but this wasn't the case for me. I first played the game, if you can call running around Kokiri Forest "playing the game," back around launch in 1998, when I was four years old. It was my older brother's Nintendo 64, and his copy of the game, which he had already completed. My adventures in Hyrule primarily consisted of exploring Hyrule Field and switching between the child and adult timelines. I even loved flipping through my brother's strategy guide to the point that my mom got it spiral bound at Kinko's.

But I never made any progress. The animation of Link pulling the Master Sword from its marble resting place was mesmerizing to me, but to be completely honest … Ganondorf terrified me too much to want to actually face him in the climactic battle. I distinctly remember a moment at summer camp a short time later, when each camper was asked to share a fear. Some were afraid of snakes. Some picked spiders or the dark. I said "Ganondorf" without a second thought, and I meant it. He was terrifying! His evil smirk when looking down on Link as he chased Zelda and Impa out of the castle was burned into my brain.
Terrifying

I started and ultimately fizzled out on a few more playthroughs on Nintendo 64, and eventually picked up a new version of Ocarina of Time for GameCube a few years later--the Legend of Zelda: Collector's Edition, which was pretty much the same experience but with a better controller. Still, I found myself struggling to get any further, and I put the game aside in favor of Super Smash Bros. I sure wish I hadn't opened it, too, considering how ridiculously valuable it is today .

It would be many years before I made another attempt, this time on 3DS. This version was marketed as a big improvement over the original Nintendo 64 release, and it's hard to deny that, even from the game's early moments. The motion controls on 3DS made aiming the slingshot remarkably easy, and the much-needed visual overhaul made the characters seem more like people. But still, despite loving what I played, I drifted away. This time, it was shortly after finishing the Forest Temple, and though I planned to go back and finish the rest of the game, that never happened.

As the years passed, I had resigned myself to the fact, or what I thought was a fact, that I would never finish Ocarina of Time. I still had a great appreciation for what it brought to the medium, but I wasn't champing at the bit to give it another try.

That was, of course, until Nintendo decided to remake the game again, this time on Nintendo Switch 2. Caught up in the excitement of so many of my friends and colleagues playing Ocarina of Time again, I decided to give it another shot--and to be completely honest, I wasn't sure things would be any different this time.

Maybe it was everyone around me getting caught up in the excitement of playing Ocarina of Time together. Maybe it was being able to sing the songs instead of having to press the buttons. It might have just been that the game had less friction this time, with the motion-controlled aiming and movable camera just making it more enjoyable to play.
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_xMM7L2XoMc

It was likely some combination of all of these factors that kept me hooked past when I would usually burn out and move on to a different game. After making it past the Forest Temple, Fire Temple, and Water Temple, it occurred to me that I was actually nearing the final battle with Ganondorf. A few hours later, I had all the Sages on board, and I made my way into Ganondorf's imposing tower.

Just from absorbing gaming pop-culture over the years, I knew to expect his aggressive organ music as I climbed to the top, but it still felt monumental. Frankly, I even already knew the strategy for beating him, but finally getting to do it myself--and then deliver the "real" final blow against his monstrous Ganon form--was like finally closing a chapter in my life. Ocarina of Time was one of the first video games I can remember watching someone play, and I probably would never have finally seen the credits roll if this remake didn't exist.
Thanks, Nintendo.

articles.headline: Backloggd urges users to change their passwords after a breach
keyFacts: Video game-logging site Backloggd urged users to change passwords after an attacker exploited a bug to access user data.
Administrator MrProg stated the breach exposed usernames, emails, hashed passwords, and IP addresses, but payment information was not affected.
Administrator MrProg is reverting all unauthorized changes made by the attacker, seeking legal guidance, and requiring users to log back in.
body: Backloggd urges users to change their passwords after a breach
The website does not store payment, government ID or financial information, so none of that was exposed.

Video game-logging site Backloggd has urged users to change their passwords after announcing a security breach. The website's administrator MrProg wrote in a post dated November 25 that "someone exploited a bug in Backloggd to gain access to the site's admin tools." As a result, the infiltrator was able to access usernames, email addresses, hashed passwords and the IP addresses users signed in from. Payment information was not affected as that's handled through Patreon.

Backloggd admin MrProg said that, while the platform uses "a strong hashing method" to mask login credentials, "weak or common passwords can sometimes be guessed from their hashes." As such, it's best for Backlogged users to change their password for the site and anywhere else they use the same one. (Take this as a reminder to opt for a strong, unique password on every single service you use. A password manager can help handle that, while passkeys and multi-factor authentication add extra layers of security to your accounts.)

MrProg apologized for the security incident. The admin took Backloggd offline as soon as they became aware of the situation to fix the bug and lock out the attacker, who also hid games and restricted some accounts. All users will need to log back in, and MrProg said they're reverting all the changes the attacker made.

"Your game logs, reviews and lists all remain intact," MrProg added. "I'm currently seeking legal guidance to ensure I handle this with absolute care and will share a full notice with more details soon." The site's operator has "already added stricter access to the admin tools and will continue to commit to stronger security features to help protect your account."

Backloggd is a site on which people can log and rate games they play, in a similar fashion to what Letterboxd does for movies. Users can track their game collection, review what they've played, create lists and follow their friends' gaming progress. Backloggd has been around for eight years and it hit 1 million users this month. A native mobile app is coming next year. Those who back the site via Patreon can now check out a beta version of the Android app.

articles.headline: Dark Eagle, America’s first operational long-range hypersonic missile battery, is ‘ready to go,’ Army honcho claims
keyFacts: Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano stated the U.S. Army's first Dark Eagle long-range hypersonic weapon battery is operational following a three-year delay.
The land-based system aims to launch missiles at 3,800 miles per hour to hit targets within 1,725 miles.
The Army is developing second and third hypersonic batteries, but Lozano declined to speculate when they will become operational.
body: After a three-year delay, the Army’s first long-range hypersonic weapon (LRHW) battery is now operational and “ready to go,” the general in charge of munitions told a defense publication.
“It is fully fielded. It is ready to go,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, director of the Rapid Capabilities and Critical Technologies Office Fires, told Breaking Defense last week.

“It is a global deployable and employable warfighting capability,” he added of the LRHW, also known as the Dark Eagle. “Those soldiers and those units have everything that they need to employ, fight and win.”
Advertisement
Fully fielded means that the advanced system has now been completely delivered and integrated across intended units.
It’s unclear when the Dark Eagle became fully fielded.

In April of this year, the military considered deploying it against Iran, with its missiles reportedly costing $15 million a pop, Bloomberg reported. But the outlet also reported last month that it still wasn’t fully fielded yet.
Advertisement
Development of hypersonic firepower, which can travel at Mach 5 or faster, has been a top priority for the Department of War because of its potential to scramble current missile defense technology.

For years, experts have warned that Russia and China have had an edge over the US in the race for development of hypersonic weaponry. America had long struggled with hypersonic development, something Secretary of War Pete Hegseth blamed on the Biden administration.

The Army originally sought to get the long-range hypersonic missile battery fielded in 2023, but ran into engineering and other development woes that delayed its completion. At one point, the Army punted its target date to September of last year, but missed that deadline as well.
Advertisement
Lozano declined to clarify whether a report from Bloomberg last month claiming that the Dark Eagle had yet to be fielded was accurate.
“[T]his is a rapidly evolving space, and things can happen very quickly,” Lozano told Breaking Defense.

“And for all the right reasons, we in the Army and we at PAE [Program Acquisition Executive] Fires are being very, very aggressive about producing, developing and fielding new capabilities that include Dark Eagle.”
Advertisement
The land-based Dark Eagle is aimed at being able to launch a missile that can fly at 3,800 miles per hour and hit targets within 1,725 miles.
The military is also working on shorter-range hypersonic systems such as Castelion’s Blackbeard, and the Navy has been developing its Conventional Prompt Strike project.

“All of our long-range fires efforts and capabilities are significantly important to the Army and to the Department of [Defense], and so they all remain a very high priority for us,” Lozano stressed to the outlet.
Advertisement
The Army is also developing a second and third LRHW battery system, but Lozano declined to speculate when they will be operational.

articles.headline: Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
keyFacts: A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is now streaming on Netflix after a seven-year break.
The show follows patrons at a Shinjuku restaurant run by an owner played by Kaoru Kobayashi.
Six of ten planned episodes are available, with new episodes releasing every Tuesday.
body: The bigger Netflix gets, the easier it is to miss stuff. This is true of all digital platforms, of course, but it’s especially true of Netflix of late, as the streaming service’s lineup now also includes a growing library of reality shows, live-programming, and even games. It makes it easy for some of the best shows to zoom right past you, unnoticed — which almost happened to me with Midnight Diner.
Netflix’s coziest show has made a very quiet return
A new season of Midnight Diner: Tokyo Stories is streaming now, though it’s easy to miss.

If you haven’t seen it, Midnight Diner is probably the most comforting thing available on Netflix. The show follows the patrons of a cozy little restaurant tucked away in the backstreets of Shinjuku, which is only open during the unusual hours of midnight to 7:00AM. This, in turn, attracts a unique blend of customers, who help each other out under the watchful eye of the shop’s owner (Kaoru Kobayashi), known only as “master.” The show aired for three seasons on Japanese TV, before being picked up by Netflix for a handful more under the subtitle Tokyo Stories.

What’s especially notable about the show’s return is the huge gap: season 2 of the Netflix iteration streamed in 2019, and it took seven years for it to come back. The break was so long that season 3’s first episode, which premiered in October, is about the restaurant’s struggles during the pandemic. There are a bunch of cute scenes of the diner’s regulars sneaking outside to check if the restaurant is open yet, and wondering if it will ever be able to. If nothing else, the break was a chance for the reliable master to finally take a vacation.

But once Midnight Diner’s new season gets going, it’s right back to everything that made it beloved. Each episode uses a different dish as a way of exploring a particular story. An overworked manga artist imagines the life he missed out on over plates of spicy konjac, while a pair of old friends reconnect while munching on pork cutlet sandwiches. What’s remarkable about the show is the way it balances being a charming, comforting watch with exploring truly difficult and heartbreaking topics. It’s the combination of sweetness and sadness that makes it work so well. It’s as likely to make you laugh as it is to make you cry.

And unlike most Netflix series, the whole season isn’t streaming all at once. Instead, new episodes come out every Tuesday; so far six of a planned 10 episodes are available. It’s a welcome way to spend an evening, as the show’s slow pace and warm sense of humanity can feel like all-too rare traits in the current streaming landscape.

But the main reason I’m even writing about Midnight Diner’s return is that it has been so easy to miss. There’s been next to no promotion for it — all I could find was a trailer on Netflix’s Japanese YouTube channel — and I only happened upon it accidentally after the initial premiere while browsing aimlessly through Netflix’s new releases. This, despite being someone who has watched and rewatched the previous seasons multiple times. You’d think I’d get a notification or something. Netflix has always been full of hidden gems, but now that it’s busier than ever, those gems are all the more hidden.

articles.headline: EA removes some live service fluff from Skate and ends seasonal structure "in favour of regular, agile content updates"
keyFacts: Developer Full Circle announced that EA is removing seasonal updates and the skate.Pass battle pass from the game Skate.
The studio stated this change will allow developers to release new features and content more frequently without waiting for a new season.
Full Circle added that the in-game currency Tix is being retired and some previously paywalled maps will no longer be locked.
body: EA is ditching seasonal updates and shaving some of the live service fluff off Skate (for some reason stylised as skate.) going forward. Normally, such news would be cause for concern. Here, the publisher assured players the transition will lead to more regular updates since devs can now push out new features without waiting for the next season to roll around.

"EA and Full Circle are committed to keep driving skate. forward. Just as a reminder, we're still very much in Early Access," the studio wrote in a new blog post. "The game is still a work in progress, and we're using this valuable time to experiment, iterate, and figure out what works best for the long-term health of the game - especially when it comes to social features and progression. Ultimately, we want to build skate. in a way that lets us roll out fresh content much faster, even if it's not totally finished yet."

Skate's fifth and final season is coming to an end on 1st December, with Full Circle embracing a different model from there on out. "We are transitioning away from the traditional seasonal cadence in favor of regular, agile content updates," it explained.

Full Circle is also throwing out the skating sim's version of a seasonal battle pass (horribly named skate.Pass) by the end of the year, and will rethink how the game's progression system works: "We've said it many times: we have a long-term future vision for skate, and this is a key part of it. Update 0.33.1 will be our very first update in this post-season era."

The move away from rigid seasonal updates "gives the development team the freedom to launch features earlier in their lifecycle," the blog post continued. "This means we can deploy work-in-progress mechanics and gather your direct feedback to continuously shape and build upon San Vansterdam. We've started this with in-game testing of features such as Spot Battles, Block Parties, and Prox Chat before rolling it out officially, and we’re going to continue with this process."

Full Circle's live service rejig also means the in-game currency Tix is being retired, and some maps will no longer be locked behind paywalls. Skate still has real-money microtransactions and a cosmetics store, though it's nice to see some of the more aggressive live service bits being plucked out.

articles.headline: Nvidia hits pause on chip shipments to Southeast Asia
keyFacts: Nvidia instructed manufacturing partners to pause server shipments to four Southeast Asian countries, according to a Journal report.
Nvidia is assessing whether regional partners meet U.S. export requirements after Chinese companies accessed chips remotely.
The Institute for Progress estimated that remote data centers supply about 24% of China's AI computing power.
body: Nvidia is under pressure to do things differently, and a new WSJ report shows how far that’s going.

According to the Journal, Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to hit pause on server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia for an unspecified period as it assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.

As for why those countries, Chinese companies have been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers there, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed — reportedly grudgingly — earlier this month. The Journal notes that the think tank Institute for Progress estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China’s AI computing power.

articles.headline: Haley Stevens' Bizarre Thanksgiving Post Sparks Fresh Wave Of Online Mockery
keyFacts: Outgoing Representative Haley Stevens faced online mockery after sharing a Thanksgiving post on social media on Wednesday.
Stevens drew condemnation from Democrats after losing her primary and endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan's Senate race.
Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed defeated Rogers in the general election after winning the Democratic primary against Stevens.
body: Outgoing Rep. Haley Stevens’ (D-Mich.) Thanksgiving post got torn apart by social media users on Wednesday, adding to a series of public gaffes the congresswoman has made in the last several weeks.

After losing her primary election, Stevens had a public falling out with the Democratic Party after endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race over her primary opponent, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.).
Progressive and establishment Democrats alike condemned Stevens’ move while lining up behind El-Sayed, who went on to defeat Rogers in the general election.
For her post on Wednesday, Stevens attempted a playful twist on one of her most viral moments from a July campaign video, which drew widespread online mockery at the time.

In the video, Stevens said she would fight for her constituents “with a little bit of joy, a little bit of enthusiasm, a little bit of energy, and a little bit of stick-it-to-’em! Because that’s the Michigan way!”
Stevens’ Thanksgiving post, which featured a picture of the congresswoman and her fiancé Jason Turkish, drew similar mockery.
“Stick a fork in the turkey — and stick it to ‘em,” Stevens’ post began.

“Grateful to live in a country where a landscaper’s daughter can serve four terms in Congress, and a legally blind guy can go to law school and spend his life helping people,” the post continued. “A country big enough for every voice — where we can disagree, respect one another, and still share the same table.”
Commenters were ready with a litany of digs to throw at Stevens, from accusing her of using AI to create the post to asking if Rogers approved the message before she posted it.

articles.headline: You’ve lived in a red state all your life. Is it wrong to pick up and move to a blue state now?
keyFacts: A Vox advice columnist responded to a reader considering moving her family from a red state to a blue state for better protections.
The columnist cited philosophical arguments showing that prioritizing a spouse's safety and well-being over general community obligations is morally appropriate.
The columnist advised the reader to create a concrete plan before moving to continue supporting red-state organizations remotely.
body: Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form . Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity:

I’m considering moving my family from a red state to a blue state. I’ve lived in a red state my whole life, and as a lesbian with a wonderful trans wife, it is hard. Moving to a blue state could give my wife and I better nondiscrimination protections, better worker protections, and better access to health care.

However, I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state. I am well aware of how the red state exodus and the red state brain drain are already affecting our community. It’s hard to weigh what may be best for my wife against what’s best for our fellow red state residents.
Dear Should I Stay or Should I Go,

I feel your question deep in my bones. Not long ago, I made the decision to move with my partner from the US to Canada, where I’m originally from. We’re also a queer couple. And we grappled with many of the same questions you’re wrestling with now.
Is it selfish to leave? If you leave, would you be putting your own family’s well-being above the well-being of your wider community? Does that mean you’re reneging on your values?

A few key philosophical ideas really helped me navigate these questions, so I’ll walk you through them. Whether you agree or disagree, they should clarify the terms in a way that makes it easier for you to decide one way or another.
Let’s start with your concern about how to weigh what’s best for your wife against what’s best for your wider community.

One strain of thought in modern philosophy — promoted by utilitarians like Peter Singer — says that we should aim to maximize the overall good, and that means doing good impartially rather than prioritizing certain people just because they happen to be our nearest and dearest. This perspective has become so influential in the past century that it’s probably shaping your thinking here, even if you’re not explicitly aware of it.
Have a question you want answered in the next Your Mileage May Vary column?
Fill out this anonymous form ! Newsletter subscribers will get my column before anyone else does and their questions will be prioritized for future editions. Sign up here!

But I want you to know that other philosophers have pushed back. Bernard Williams, a staunch critic of utilitarianism, argued that it can actually be totally normal and morally appropriate to show partiality toward our loved ones.

In a famous passage, Williams said that if a man sees two people drowning, and one is his wife and the other is a stranger, and he pauses to consider whether rescuing his wife would maximize the overall good more than rescuing the stranger, he has had “ one thought too many .”

Williams argued that moral agency does not sit in a contextless vacuum — it is always some specific person’s agency, and as specific people we have specific commitments. When you got together with your wife, you made a commitment to ensuring her well-being, over and above your general wish for all people everywhere to be well. Utilitarianism says you have to consider everyone’s well-being equally, with no special treatment for your own family members — but to Williams, that’s just an absurd demand. It alienates you from a core part of yourself, destroying your integrity as a moral agent.

According to this view, putting your wife’s safety first isn’t some moral lapse that should embarrass you. Honoring special obligations to our nearest and dearest is actually part of what makes a life ethical.

Besides, even though living an ethical life does sometimes involve being willing to sacrifice some of our own well-being, it’s important to recognize that everybody exists at a different vulnerability level. We shouldn’t expect someone who’s trans to take on risk to the same degree as someone who is not particularly marginalized or endangered.

Given the assault on trans rights in recent years, I’d be really skeptical of anyone who tries to argue that you and your wife have a moral obligation to stay put and “fight the good fight” if she’d be happier and safer elsewhere. Mind you, I also want to caution you to consider all the factors that go into making a happy life before you come to any decision about moving. If your wife has a robust and loving community of friends in your current red state, but knows nobody in the blue state you’re thinking of moving to, she may end up unhappier there on balance. (Plus, as the recent midterms showed, red states don’t necessarily stay red , and even blue states can pass anti-trans rights ballot measures .)

I also think a bigger reframe is in order here. You say, “I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state.” But would it really? I’d argue that the key consideration is: Where can you keep fighting the longest? The hardest? The most effectively?

The work of contemporary philosopher Lisa Tessman is instructive here. In her book Burdened Virtues , she argues that situations of oppression can demand certain traits of people — like sustained anger at injustice, fierce loyalty to one’s group, constant vigilance and sensitivity to others’ suffering — that can damage the people who embody them even though they are real virtues. These traits can undermine the well-being of the bearers over time, keeping them from flourishing. What’s more, they can potentially even warp their bearers’ moral character — for example, when anger grows into an all-consuming state.

You said that you’ve lived in a red state your whole life and found it hard. So I think it’s worth asking yourself: Are the traits you’ve had to develop under those circumstances — however virtuous they may be — actually eroding your ability to keep showing up, both for yourself and for your wider community, in the way you’d like? If you feel that, say, constant vigilance is starting to take its toll, moving might give you a mental reset that allows you to be more — not less — active in enacting your values.

Plus, a quick look at the historical record can defuse the idea that leaving a place means “abandoning the good fight.” Consider what happened in the Great Migration, the exodus of Black Americans from the Jim Crow South. Did those migrants “abandon the good fight”? Absolutely not. Once in the North and West, they built up political power and institutions that ended up feeding into and supporting the civil rights movement .

The point is not that the two situations are exact parallels — they aren’t. The point is that when people leave a place, they can choose to use the affordances of their new home in a way that helps their old home. So, although worries about a red state exodus and red state brain drain are totally understandable, I don’t think they decide the question of whether a move would be net-negative or net-positive for your wider community.
What will decide that is what you choose to do with your newfound resources — including, plausibly, an increased sense of safety, security, and mental health — if you do relocate.

Life gets busy really fast, especially after a big move. (I should know — months after moving, I still haven’t gotten around to putting up any art on my walls!) So, if you leave your home state, my strong recommendation to you is this: Make a plan, in advance, for how you will keep fighting the good fight once you reach your new destination. Will you organize remotely? Can you connect right now with the relevant leaders at red state groups you want to support? Which organizations will you donate to, how much will you give, and when?
To boost accountability and prevent mission drift, be as concrete and specific as possible, discuss your plans aloud with your wife, and write them down.
And once you’ve done all this? My dear, let go of your guilt and live.
Bonus: What I’m reading

I loved this Aeon essay about “love with nowhere to go.” It notes that, although we have established social scripts for grief that arises in the wake of a death, we don’t have practices for recognizing and working through grief that’s not death-related. That’s a problem because “when we are unable to honor other profound losses, we become strangers to ourselves.”

Noema published an absolutely wonderful piece by Atoosa Kasirzadeh on how AI is changing math — and how it should! In fact, the AI revolution can have the great effect of reorienting the field to things that really matter according to humans. In my opinion, this is a model for how many other fields should adapt, so it’s really worth reading even if you’re not “a math person.”

Most Westerners don’t have a good window into how people in China think about AI. So I was excited to see Persona publishing Jen Zhu on why the West’s habit of thinking about AI as an arms race misses the mark from a Chinese perspective. “When you watch a competitor sprint, you assume the finish line is the same as yours,” she writes. “But China is not running America’s race. It is continuing a 3,000-year-old project of ordering society as a single organism, harmonized rather than unleashed.”

articles.headline: ZDNET’s best headphones of 2026: These two pairs left us impressed
keyFacts: ZDNET selected the Beats 360 as its top headphone of 2026, with the Sennheiser Momentum 5 chosen as runner-up.
The Beats 360 features interchangeable modular earpads that alter functionality for workout or casual listening settings.
Sennheiser says its runner-up Momentum 5 features up to 57 hours of playtime and an easily self-repairable battery.
body: Choosing the best headphones of the year isn’t as cut-and-dry a process as other tech categories. All of our ears are different, so what sounds good is ultimately subjective. However, there are plenty of other benchmarks beyond sound quality and noise-canceling performance that make a pair of headphones stand out to us and receive our Editors’ Choice award.

We’ve awarded headphones that debut with significant, tangible upgrades over their predecessors, such as the Sennheiser Momentum 5 and the Sonos Ace Ultra. Headphones with a unique and useful feature, like the Beats 360’s purpose-changing earpads, also catch our attention.

We also like headphones that embrace the latest wireless and audio technologies, such as LE Audio and Auracast, which is exactly what the Sony WF-1000XM6 does. I’ve had a chance to go hands-on with dozens of headphones this year, but these two stand out for their combination of features, audio quality, and value relative to price.
The best headphones of 2026:
Beats 360
Get it now
Expert Take

The Beats 360 earned their spot as ZDNET’s pick for best headphones of the year, thanks to their unique take on earpad modularity, innovative audio engineering, sweat- and water-resistance, and native compatibility with Apple and Android. Beats created a pair of modular headphones that change functionality when you switch their earpads: the Performance Knit cushions are sweat-wicking and suited for exercise, while the UltraPlush cushions provide a comfortable, casual, and immersive listening experience.
Read our review: Beats 360

Since I got the Beats 360, I’ve retired my AirPods Pro 3 at the gym. Upgraded GymKit functionality in iOS 27 allows me to track cardio workouts from my iPhone, and I don’t have to worry about the 360 slipping off my head; I just don’t need my AirPods anymore. The Beats 360 include the Performance Knit cushions with purchase, and a pair of UltraPlush cushions is $50. That’ll bring your total to $400, but you’re getting two headphones in one.
Our runner-up:
Sennheiser Momentum 5
Get it now
Expert Take

Sennheiser’s Momentum 5 debuted with significant upgrades over the Momentum 4, including a more detailed equalizer, a sleeker design, Dolby Atmos optimization, and improved ANC, making it more competitive with its contemporaries from Sony, Bose, and Apple. Sennheiser doesn’t beat any of its premium competitors in ANC, but it’s very close. Still, the Momentum 5 has something its competitors don’t: an easily self-repairable battery.
Read our review: Sennheiser Momentum 5

I love the Momentum 5’s detailed and balanced sound, hours-long comfort, and marathon battery life, which Sennheiser says delivers 57 hours of uninterrupted playtime. The Momentum 5 supports several hi-res AptX codecs and lossless audio via a wired USB-C connection. Regardless of whether your devices are Android, iOS, Windows, or anything else, you can access the Momentum 5’s full suite of features.

articles.headline: A rising political star in China is the latest victim of Xi’s purge
keyFacts: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining is under investigation for suspected discipline and law violations, state media reported.
Chen is the fourth Politburo member purged in under two years amid President Xi Jinping's power consolidation effort.
The downfall comes ahead of next year's Communist Party Congress, where Xi is expected to extend his rule.
body: He was on the rise among China’s political elite, hosting tech leaders and senior American officials. But now Shanghai party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s influential politburo, appears to be the latest senior official brought down by President Xi Jinping’s sweeping purge.

The hammer unexpectedly came down on Chen in the form of a two-line bulletin on the Xinhua news agency Tuesday: He is “suspected of serious violations of Party discipline and law and is currently under disciplinary review and supervisory investigation” — a common euphemism for corruption crackdowns on ruling Communist Party officials under Xi.
Public announcements such as these usually mark the end of a political career in China. Chen has made no public statement.

He is the fourth politburo member to be purged in less than two years, part of a broader crackdown that has swept aside top military leaders as Xi consolidates power. He is set to extend his rule next year, at a party congress that is held once every five years and looms over the preceding months.
But Chen’s abrupt downfall took many close observers of China by surprise, given his profile and career path would usually point to a bright future.

“He was potentially going to the highest level, which would be the standing committee. And I think from a lot of Western observers, people thought he had even better prospects,” Damien Ma, the Singapore-based director of the Carnegie China think tank, told NBC News.
Xi’s pursuit of loyalty

Some analysts have speculated that Xi, increasingly viewed as likely to rule for life, may have been purging a viable replacement. Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London, said however that Chen was “someone who could rise further but not as a successor.”

Chen, a 62-year-old technocrat known as a friend of foreign business and an advocate for AI, was an environmental scientist who studied in London and swiftly rose through the party’s ranks. He served as China’s environmental minister, Beijing’s mayor and the party secretary in Shanghai — a post once held by Xi and widely considered a stepping stone to bigger things.

Just last month, Chen hosted Apple Chairman Tim Cook, welcoming the U.S. tech giant to “make full use of Shanghai’s strengths” and bring more products to the city, a financial and cultural hub that has long served as a connection between China and the international community.
In his last public appearance last week, during a tour of a shipping facility, Chen called for advancing the industry’s digital transformation.
By Wednesday, Chen’s name has been removed from some official websites. A webpage on the Shanghai government site showing that meeting with Cook is now showing a 404 message, or not found.

Chen is just the latest senior official in the crosshairs of Xi’s long-running anti-corruption campaign and emphasis on party discipline, which analysts say is as much about loyalty as it is about reform.

“It is a warning to all technocrats, as Chen was a rising star among technocrats and had no apparent failures in a technocratic way. So, message is: adhere to strict party discipline and demonstrate unquestionable loyalty to Xi or else,” Tsang said.

The party’s Central Committee, which has about 200 mostly male leaders, vowed to “ensure more rigorous discipline enforcement, and make full use of discipline as a guide, restraint, guarantee, and incentive” at its closed-door gathering, the fifth plenum, last month.

“What they’ve been building as part of this discipline machine over the last 15 years is to kind of implement their sort of internal operating system of how they deal with, let’s say, bad eggs within the party,” Ma, of Carnegie China, said.

“The top leadership is normalizing this anti-corruption, this self-cleansing,” Ma said. “It is now a normal part of what the party expects, and they’re trying to embed that over time and down to every single level,” he added.

The Chinese government has not announced any charges against Chen, who was the youngest member of the country’s elite decision-making body. The 24-member Politburo was unveiled in 2022 but is now down to 21 members after the purges. Last month, top general Zhang Shengmin was elevated to the body in a rare addition.

Chen’s undoing comes a year before the party’s top leadership is reshuffled at the 21st Communist Party Congress, when Xi is expected to solidify control even further and cement another five-year term at the helm of the country.
From London to Shanghai

Born in 1964, Chen studied at the prestigious Tsinghua university, long a major pipeline for senior party officials and where he served as president from 2012 to 2015. His name has now been removed from Tsinghua’s online list of former presidents.
After studying at Tsinghua in the 1980s, he moved for a decade to Britain, where he obtained a doctorate from Imperial College London in 1993.
Chen returned to Tsinghua’s environmental science and engineering department in 1998 before being named the university’s president in 2012, according to an official biography.
He’s authored dozens of papers, including on carbon emission reduction and water quality monitoring.

The relatively young Chen would ride around campus on his bike and built a reputation for pushing institutional reforms in his three years at the helm of the university, according to an article in People’s Digest, a magazine affiliated with the People’s Daily, the community party’s official newspaper.

The article, titled “From University President to Cabinet Minister,” was published in 2015, the same year he was picked to lead the Environmental Protection Ministry. In 2017, Chen became mayor of the capital, Beijing, where he oversaw the 2022 Winter Olympics during the Covid pandemic.
Later that year he was transferred to Shanghai and became the party chief, a coveted role that Xi took on himself in 2007 before becoming the country’s leader in 2013.
There, he became heavily involved with the tech industry, regularly hosting CEOs and advocating for more investment into Shanghai, where the World AI Conference was hosted earlier this year.

Chen hosted Elon Musk in 2023 to discuss Tesla’s operations in the city. Last year, he accompanied Xi to an AI hub there. And last month, Chen met with several European tech leaders, in addition to hosting Cook.
Alongside the top post in Shanghai, Chen also was elected for a five-year term as a member of the Politburo, China’s elite decision-making body headed by Xi.
While the Politburo is not the absolute apex of power, he was seen as a contender the much-smaller Politburo’s Standing Committee, which is made up of the country’s highest ranking officials.

“If you’re party secretary of one of the four big municipalities, Beijing, Shanghai, Chongqing and Tianjin, you have pretty good prospects. That’s sort of an indication that you’re on your way up,” Ma said.

Whether or not Chen’s ousting deals a blow to the country’s technology ambitions and its race for dominance in artificial intelligence, remains to be seen, Ma said. But either way, his downfall will force a rethink among those seeking to predict the route to power in modern China.
“Part of it is thinking through what is really the new criteria to get to the top, and they may not be what we thought just a few months ago,” Ma added.
